content.text: Writing is usually solitary. It does not have to be. Foma lets two (or more) writers work on the same project from their own computers, each holding a full copy of the manuscript — no extra accounts, no servers, no subscription. The GitHub connection you made at the start of this chapter is the entire infrastructure.
A co-writer needs the same two things you have: Foma, and a free GitHub account.

content.text: Once your co-writer accepts, they appear in this window's collaborator list. The same window is where you revoke a pending invitation or remove a collaborator later — removal takes away their access to the shared GitHub project space, though they keep whatever local copy they have already downloaded.
NOTE: An invitation grants full writing access. This is a co-author's seat, not a reader's — invite writers you trust with the manuscript.
When someone invites you, Foma notifies you in three places: behind the bell on the welcome screen, under

to jump straight to your invitations from anywhere.
Each invitation names the writer who sent it and the exact repository you are being invited into. Click

— an invitation never interrupts a writing session.

NOTE: "Cloning" is GitHub's way of expressing that it is creating a local copy of a project that lives on the server. It just means that a copy will be downloaded to your computer from the remote location.
Day to day, co-writing feels exactly like writing alone: draft, remember,
. Every sync downloads your co-writer's latest work first, then uploads yours, and Foma weaves the two together.
When a co-writer has pushed work you have not seen yet, a small dot appears on the GitHub icon in the title bar. Sync to pull their writing in.

NOTE: Foma merges at the level of blocks and paragraphs, not whole files. You can both write in the same scene at the same time, and as long as you are not rewriting the very same paragraph, both contributions land cleanly side by side.

To bring one into the open, hover it in the Comments panel and click the share icon — the comment moves into the project's shared channel, where your co-writers can read it, reply to it, and resolve it after their next sync. Your GitHub avatar rides along, so everyone knows which margin notes belong to whom.

A small chip beside the scene title tells you when the open scene has shared comments waiting, and it stays accent-colored until you have read them. Private comments stay private unless you explicitly share them.
